documentation.range: This species has a broad distribution across New Guinea, being absent only from mountainous regions. It is present on the offshore islands of Misol, Salawati, and Schouten in West Papua Province, and Yapen in Papua Province (Böhme 2003). The Aru Islands and Biak are recognized to hold other species within this group, treated within Varanus prasinus by Böhme (2003). There is no evidence that this species occurs in the Aru Islands (D. Bennett pers. comm. 2015). It has also been recorded on the Torres Strait islands of Boigu, Dauan, Mabuyag, Mer, Mua and Saibai and is predicted to occur on several of the other islands (Lavery et al. 2012). Australian records are now referred to a different species related to V. prasinus, Varanus keithhorni. Although anecdotal records unsupported by specimens suggest that true V. prasinus may occur in the Iron Range of northern Australia (F. Parker pers. comm. 2014), this is doubted by specialists working in this area (P. Couper pers. comm. 2017). It is known to occur from sea level to 830 m asl.
documentation.population: This species is common and widespread in New Guinea.
documentation.habitats: This species inhabits monsoon, rain and palm forests, mangrove swamps, lagoons and cocoa plantations. As long as trees and prey items are present, it will probably persist in other plantation or modified habitats (G. Shea pers. comm. 2014). This is a highly specialized tree-dwelling lizard, using its prehensile tail as a fifth limb. Like other arboreal varanid species of Papua that prefer microhabitats along tree trunks and huge branches this species inhabits dense vegetation with predominantly small trees, lots of vines, and leafy vegetation and the periphery of treetops. The diet of this species includes mainly arthropods, but also frogs, geckos, lizards, a variety of insects, small birds and mammals, and eggs (Philipp and Philipp 2007). Captive animals will occasionally take vegetable and fruit matter, included in the list of food items provided by Philipp and Philipp (2007), but these lizards lack any adaptation to digest cellulose and these items are unlikely to form a natural part of the diet (D. Bennett pers. comm. 2015, Losos and Greene 1988).
documentation.threats: It is unlikely that any major threats are impacting this species. It is present in the international pet trade but it is unlikely that current harvest levels pose a significant threat, and the species is captive-bred.
documentation.measures: This species is listed under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) and has protected status in Indonesian New Guinea (Natusch and Lyons 2012). This species probably occurs in protected areas in New Guinea.
documentation.use_trade: Most varanid species are popular in the international pet trade. This is especially true for the Papuan species (Yuwono 1998). Pernetta (2009) noted that fourteen countries exported this species and that 7,497 lizards were exported between 1975 and 2005. Natusch and Lyons (2012) noted the trade of this species from Jayapura, Merauke and the Vogelkop. Eleven, three and fifty-two individuals (respectively) of this species were recorded at wildlife traders between September 2010 and April 2011. This species is listed under CITES and has protected status in Indonesia. There is no export quota for this species.
documentation.rationale: Varanus prasinus has been assessed as Least Concern. It has a broad distribution in New Guinea. It has been recorded in wide variety of habitats and is not affected by any significant threats.
